transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-06-05
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~78 minutes
Attendees: Laura Kim (Redwood AE), Marcus Li (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (HorizonAI - Staff ML Eng), Daniel Ruiz (HorizonAI - Infra Eng), Sam Whitaker (HorizonAI - CTO)

Summary:
Quick technical deep dive focussing on GPU runtime profiling for HorizonAI's LLM workloads. Main topics: kernel selection heuristics, TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM tradeoffs, CUDA graphs / cudagraphs warmup, KV cache behavior and prefix caching, batching strategies and latency SLOs, quantization impact (FP16/INT8), on-prem/VPC constraints. Agreement to run side-by-side microbenchmarks and share traces; Redwood to provide perf runbook and quantization recommendations.

Topics: kernel selection, tensorrt-llm, vllm, cudagraphs, kv cache, batching, quantization, vpc/on-prem

Action items (quick list in call): see metadata field

Transcript Body:
[00:00:00] Laura: Hey everybody thanks for joining, afternoon for us, I think morning for you Sam, uh we'll do quick intros and then jump straight into the profiling notes. Marcus is gonna lead with a few traces we collected on a sample model similar to yours.
[00:00:18] Sam: Morning, yeah thanks Laura, appreciate it.
[00:00:22] Priya: Hi all, Priya here, I'll be primary contact for the model side. We sent over a smaller HF checkpoint earlier this week, did you get that?
[00:00:30] Laura: Yep, we pulled it, thanks. Marcus, you wanna start?
[00:00:33] Marcus: Sure. Quick context: Horizon's primary workload is a 16k token summarization flow, average ~1.8k, p95 around 9k, batch sizes small for latency SLOs but high qps. We ran both vLLM (community build) and TensorRT-LLM on A100 80GB nodes in our lab, with cudagraphs enabled. The traces I'll show are from the 8k sequence sim.
[00:01:05] Daniel: Quick question on infra: we're on GCP with private VPC and strict egress rules, gonna be on-prem later this year for some regulated customers. So any VPC/on-prem caveats matter.
[00:01:18] Marcus: Absolutely, we'll call out where ops changes are needed.
[00:01:22] Marcus: All right slide 1 - overall perf. On the vLLM side, we saw consistently higher latency tail due to more frequent tokenizer + scheduler interactions; TensorRT-LLM gave lower median and p95 for long sequences when cudagraphs were warmed. But initial cold start was worse because cudagraphs compilation and kernel link.
[00:01:55] [00:02:00] Priya: When you say "cudagraphs warmed" do you mean prebuild at deployment time or runtime warmup? We can't afford a long cold start for ephemeral workloads.
[00:02:10] Marcus: Good call. There are two patterns: prebuilding graphs at deployment for your common shapes and sequence lengths, or dynamic recording at runtime. Prebuild needs you to know the typical seq lengths and batch shapes — else you get graph bloat. For Horizon's distribution we'd recommend a small set of cand shapes: 256/1024/4096/8192 for a 16k capable model.
[00:02:44] [00:03:00] Laura: Also to note the runtime in dedicated nodes we can pin to reserved capacity and do scheduled warmups during low traffic windows to keep graphs resident. On-prem you can do the same but requires startup hooks.
[00:03:20] Daniel: For our VPC private deployment, what's the ops impact of TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM? We worry about driver/tooling compatibility and kernel dependencies.
[00:03:30] Marcus: TensorRT-LLM is more prescriptive: it brings TensorRT kernels and uses tensorrt-llm plugin kernels which are optimized but sensitive to CUDA / driver versions. vLLM is more flexible, using Triton or pytorch kernels depending on build; it's easier to iterate but we saw more variance in kernel selection causing p95 spikes. So ops tradeoff: stability + faster steady-state with TRT-LLM vs flexibility with vLLM.
[00:03:58] [00:04:20] Priya: I'm worried about model features like LoRA adapters and custom ops, will TensorRT-LLM handle that out of the box?
[00:04:30] Marcus: Not always. TRT-LLM requires either converter support or custom plugin work. In our experience small adapter layers need conversion; more complex custom ops require engineering. If you rely heavily on LoRA at runtime, vLLM path can be faster to get started. We can enumerate conversion steps in the runbook.
[00:04:52] [00:05:00] Sam: Could you walk through kernel selection heuristics — you mentioned an automatic selection step?
[00:05:06] Marcus: Yeah. At runtime we (Redwood runtime) look at model topology (attention block layouts, rotary/hybrid positional embeddings), tensor shapes per layer across seq length, and micro-benchmark a few candidate kernels — basically a small runtime calibration. Then we pick the fastest kernel per op. That calibration cost is usually a couple hundred ms per op but amortized across long sequences. With cudagraphs, kernel choice gets baked into the graph.
[00:05:40] [00:06:00] Priya: So calibration can add jitter to first few requests?
[00:06:04] Marcus: Exactly. We try to do calibration offline at deploy time or during warmup to avoid on-path hits. For multi-tenant hosted API we have a background calibration queue to avoid user latency impact.
[00:06:18] [00:06:30] Daniel: How do you handle KV cache memory fragmentation? We saw OOMs when switching between 2k and 12k sequences on the same instance.
[00:06:36] Marcus: Memory fragmentation is a big one. Two tactics: a) use a slab allocator tuned for KV cache to avoid small alloc/free churn, b) pre-allocate max kv cache for pinned model instances you expect, and manage by eviction. On A100 80GB you can reserve headroom for concurrent sessions, but on smaller cards you might need offload or split shards. We also saw issues when host pinned memory exceeded numa limits — so NUMA-aware allocator matters on multi-socket boxes.
[00:07:12] [00:07:30] Priya: Any logs/metrics you'd recommend we surface to track this?
[00:07:34] Marcus: Token-level memory usage, per-request KV allocation, fragmentation ratio, failed allocs count, and per-layer scratch space usage. We'll include counters in the runbook.
[00:07:46] [00:08:00] Laura: Quick interjection — we once saw an unexpected p95 spike because nvrtc-JIT was triggered on a stray custom op; turned out to be a stray dynamic shape. So static shapes wherever possible.
[00:08:12] [00:08:30] Sam: Let's talk batching — our product needs ~50ms tail for short queries, but also bursty bulk summarization jobs. How do you balance batching for throughput vs tail latency?
[00:08:40] Marcus: There's a suite of knobs: max_batch_size, latency SLO budget, adaptive batching window, and a priority queueing policy. For your short queries we recommend a small fast-path cluster with batch size 1-4 and pre-allocated KV to minimize jitter, and a separate high-throughput pool for batch jobs. Smart routing can send requests by latency class. Also micro-batching within the runtime can combine prefixes using prefix caching to reduce work.
[00:09:12] [00:09:30] Priya: Prefix caching — do you do prefix dedupe across requests? We have many repeated prompts.
[00:09:36] Marcus: Yes, we do both prefix KV caching and shared prefix lookup. There's an optional LRU cache that stores recent prefix KV slices keyed by a hashed prompt prefix. That reduces tokens computed but increases memory pressure; it's a tradeoff. For Horizon with many repeated onboarding prompts it's a big win.
[00:09:58] [00:10:15] Daniel: Any consistency concerns with prefix cache and user session isolation?
[00:10:20] Marcus: We namespace caches per customer or per tenant ID to avoid cross-tenant leakage. We also TTL entries and can opt-out for sensitive sessions.
[00:10:30] [00:10:45] Priya: Back to cudagraphs — what's the warmup pattern you recommend for the 16k model?
[00:10:52] Marcus: Prebuild graphs for a small shape set: 256/1024/4096/8192 as I said; then at runtime, record a few dynamic graphs for outliers. Warmup script should run a few iterations per seq shape to trigger kernel and cudagraph caches and to ensure memory placements are nearby. Note that cudagraphs cache entries are sensitive to comms topology (NVLink vs PCIe) so your on-prem pods must match the recording environment.
[00:11:30] [00:11:45] Sam: Are there known performance deltas between nvlink-connected multi-gpu vs single large 80GB instance?
[00:11:52] Marcus: Yes. NVLink multi-GPU with model sharding can have higher throughput for huge sequences but increases synchronization overhead and can hurt  tail latency due to cross-device sync. A single 80GB A100 can be simpler for latency SLOs since everything is local to one device, but cost-per-token can be higher. We'll include cost/latency curves in the benchmark sheet.
[00:12:18] [00:12:30] Priya: What about quantization — FP16 vs INT8? Our ops team wants max cost savings.
[00:12:36] Marcus: FP16 is safe for most transformer models with minimal quality degradation; INT8 can give big cost wins but needs careful calibration and per-layer scaling. For certain attention patterns INT8 can introduce hallucination regressions. Our recommended approach: start FP16, run evals on your prompt/answer set for quality delta; if acceptable, try PTQ int8 with per-channel scales and run regression tests. We'll include example accuracy vs perf curves.
[00:13:12] [00:13:30] Priya: Any gotchas on the TRT-LLM int8 path?
[00:13:34] Marcus: TRT int8 quant uses calibration tables and sometimes needs fine-tuning of activation ranges; also some ops aren't supported so TRT may fallback to FP16 for those layers — which complicates perf expectations. vLLM int8 pipelines (like bitsandbytes quant) are more flexible but may need custom kernels for peak perf.
[00:13:58] [00:14:15] Sam: Security question — for VPC/private deployment, how are keys/KMS handled and are there audit logs for inference requests?
[00:14:22] Laura: Redwood Private supports KMS/HSM integrations, and we can ship an agent that writes signed audit logs to your S3/GCS bucket. For on-prem we support local HSM integration; we'll share the compliance pack.
[00:14:36] [00:14:50] Daniel: Network egress: cudagraphs prebuild needs internet? We can't allow egress from the cluster.
[00:14:58] Marcus: It doesn't need egress; cudagraphs are local compilation artifacts. The only egress would be if you pull models from HF or a build image; for closed envs we provide an offline bundle and install guide.
[00:15:10] [00:15:30] Priya: Can you explain a little more about kernel selection failures? We saw fallback to a very slow kernel in one of our runs.
[00:15:36] Marcus: Usually due to unsupported tensor layout or unexpected dtype. The runtime has a fallback registry: if the fast kernel errors out (shape mismatch, unsupported op), it falls back to a generic kernel. The fallback path is tested but slower. We log kernel selection and fallback reasons; key is to capture traces so we can patch kernel selection rules or add conversion steps.
[00:16:00] [00:16:15] Laura: Marcus, can you show that nsight trace snippet?
[00:16:18] [00:16:30] Marcus: Yeah sharing screen. (screen share) Here: you can see the heavy time in attention matmul at layer 18 when sequence hits 8k - note the kernel chosen is a generic cuBLAS matmul due to an odd packed QKV layout. We fixed that in the converter by reshaping QKV to contiguous layout and we saw 2.3x speedup.
[00:16:58] [00:17:10] Priya: That matches an issue we saw. Our exporter kept a packed qkv to save memory.
[00:17:18] Marcus: Packed QKV sometimes helps memory but trades off kernel compatibility. We'll add a conversion step that unpacks QKV for runtime if the perf delta is worth it; that's in the runbook decision matrix.
[00:17:36] [00:17:50] Daniel: Regarding CUDA and driver versions, what versions do you recommend for TRT-LLM?
[00:17:56] Marcus: For TRT-LLM on A100, we recommend CUDA 12.x with the matching NVIDIA driver that supports TensorRT 9.x (we'll put exact pinned versions in the doc). For vLLM we had success on CUDA 11.8 too but some newer kernels perform better on 12.x. The main point: pin the stack and avoid mixing driver/runtime versions across nodes.
[00:18:25] [00:18:45] Priya: For on-prem, if we want to do a full POC, what's the minimal infra?
[00:18:50] Marcus: One 80GB A100 node with NVMe for model artifacts + 128GB host RAM for KV cache is a good start for single-node latency tests. For sharded throughput tests, 4x A100 with NVLink and a fast RDMA network. We'll help size based on your expected qps/seq length.
[00:19:12] [00:19:30] Sam: About observability — token-level traces are helpful but noisy. What traces do you send to the console?
[00:19:36] Marcus: We sample token traces and send aggregated token latency histograms, KV miss rates, per-model kernel selection summaries, cudagraphs cache hit rate, and memory pressure metrics. You can increase sampling for POC runs.
[00:19:58] [00:20:10] Priya: Any recommendations for benchmarking methodology to compare TRT-LLM vs vLLM fairly?
[00:20:16] Marcus: Yes, we recommend: 1) identical model weights and identical tokenization/config, 2) warm each runtime with the same warmup script (same seq shapes), 3) run steady-state long enough to observe tail (30-60 mins for p95), 4) capture nsight and nvprof traces for a few representative requests, 5) track quality on a holdout prompt set. We'll include a checklist and a benchmark sheet.
[00:20:50] [00:21:05] Daniel: For POC runs on our VPC, we need an offline installer.
[00:21:10] Laura: We'll package an offline bundle and step-by-step install.
[00:21:18] [00:21:30] Marcus: A couple more micro details — attention kernel choices: flash attention kernels outperform standard matmul for long sequences but require contiguous memory layout and newer GPU architectures. If your model uses rotary embeddings, some kernels are faster because they fuse rotaries with attention. These micro-kernel choices are where we get major wins.
[00:21:58] [00:22:15] Priya: So for our 16k model, flash attention + cudagraphs + TRT kernels sounds best if we can convert.
[00:22:22] Marcus: In many cases yes, but conversion complexity and int8 support may influence. That's why we do a two-arm POC.
[00:22:34] [00:22:50] Sam: Any hard numbers you can share now?
[00:22:52] Marcus: Rough numbers from lab runs: for an 8k sequence on A100 80GB, TensorRT-LLM w/ cudagraphs: median latency ~1.8s, p95 ~2.4s; vLLM w/ cudagraphs: median ~2.1s, p95 ~3.2s. With cold-start these numbers inflate — cudagraphs compile added 10-30s on first run unless prebuilt. Quantization to FP16 gave ~1.2x speedup; int8 gave ~1.8-2.3x in some layers but mixed. These are indicative; we'll run your model for exact numbers.
[00:23:34] [00:23:50] Priya: Those p95s are in line with expectations. We want to get p95 under 2s for user-facing flows.
[00:23:56] Marcus: We can get there with dedicated latency pool, prebuilt graphs and a bit of conversion.
[00:24:08] [00:24:30] (--- Mid-call: deeper profiling snippets and shared links ---)
[00:24:45] Marcus: I'm pasting a link in the chat: perf sheet & nsight snippet (link: https://redwood.example.com/perf/hzn-06-05) (note: placeholder).
[00:25:00] [00:25:15] Priya: Got it, thanks.
[00:25:20] [00:25:30] Marcus: Another thing: batching windows — if you set adaptive window to 5ms you get microbatching gains for small requests without hitting long tail too often, but it's hardware dependent.
[00:25:46] [00:26:00] Sam: On the quant side, how do you measure quality regression? We need automatic regression alerts.
[00:26:06] Marcus: We run prompt-based evals with automatic metrics (perplexity, ROUGE, semantic similarity) and a human-annotated sample set for critical flows. Redwood Optimize can hook into your eval set and create regression alerts when quality drops beyond threshold.
[00:26:26] [00:26:40] Priya: For int8, can we do per-batch fallback to FP16 if quality drops?
[00:26:45] Marcus: Yes, runtime can do per-batch or per-request fallback. But this increases complexity and could make perf less predictable; better to gate int8 to safe models or rollout gradually.
[00:26:58] [00:27:10] Daniel: Any suggestions on monitoring GPU SM utilization vs memory bound?
[00:27:16] Marcus: Track SM occupancy, achieved occupancy, mem throughput, and kernel durations. If SM utilization is high but mem throughput low, likely compute-bound; if mem throughput saturated, look at kernel fusion or layout.
[00:27:36] [00:27:50] Priya: Can you help set up a small automated benchmark that runs nightly and reports drift?
[00:27:56] Laura: Yes we'll include a CI template.
[00:28:05] [00:28:20] (--- They discuss a specific flaky run where cudagraphs cache invalidated due to a different allocator flag ---)
[00:28:36] Marcus: Cudagraphs hash includes allocator config and stream flags — changing allocator at runtime invalidates cached graphs. That's a common gotcha.
[00:28:50] [00:29:05] Priya: Does Redwood ship an allocator?
[00:29:10] Marcus: We have a recommended allocator; it's in runbook, and for Private deployments we can provide the agent that sets the allocator defaults.
[00:29:22] [00:29:40] Sam: We need to know licensing implications for TensorRT-LLM, is there any additional license cost?
[00:29:46] Laura: TensorRT is NVIDIA-licensed but generally allowed for deployments; we will flag any enterprise licensing needs in the procurement packet.
[00:29:58] [00:30:10] (--- Then a long section where Marcus walks through an nsight timeline and points out kernel durations, memory stalls, and an attention kernel optimization that removed a memcpy ---)
[00:50:15] Marcus: Here you can see the cudagraphs step — notice the initial recording has a few large memcpy ops then on subsequent runs they're absent, that's the graph capture effect. Also you can see the kernel fusion reduces launch overhead.
[00:50:45] Priya: Is there risk of correctness regressions from graph-fused kernels?
[00:50:52] Marcus: Very low if conversion is correct; unit tests catch most. Still we recommend QA on a holdout prompt set after conversion.
[00:51:10] [00:51:30] Daniel: One more infra Q: for private deployment, do we need to expose any ports for monitoring?
[00:51:36] Laura: We can stream metrics over your internal network; no inbound ports required. Logs can be written to a customer-controlled bucket.
[00:51:50] [00:52:10] (--- Final section: roadmap and planning ---)
[01:05:00] Marcus: To summarize technical recommendations: 1) start POC with TRT-LLM and vLLM parallel runs on one 80GB node, 2) prebuild a small matrix of cudagraphs shapes, 3) convert packed QKV to contiguous where it causes fallbacks, 4) begin with FP16 and run quality checks before INT8, 5) provision a small low-latency pool for user-facing queries.
[01:05:40] Sam: Timeline — we'd like a tight 3-week POC. Is that doable?
[01:05:48] Laura: Yes, we can scope a 3-week POC: week 1 infra + install + warmup, week 2 perf runs and traces, week 3 quality eval + recommendations.
[01:06:02] Priya: Ok we'll aim for that. I'll share the model link and sample load shapes.
[01:06:12] Laura: Great. We'll follow up with the runbook and benchmark sheet. Marcus anything to add?
[01:06:18] Marcus: I'll attach the nsight traces and a short checklist of conversion steps.
[01:06:24] Sam: Thanks everyone, this was helpful.
[01:06:30] Laura: Thanks all. Quick recap of next steps in chat.
[01:06:40] (end)

Notes about transcript: Some minor transcription errors may exist (product names, acronyms) and speaker overlap occasional. Links shared in chat are placeholders for internal artifacts.
